analysis.one_liner: Protects doctors who provide legal abortion, contraception, and IVF care from state and private interference.
analysis.headline: Backed by 30 senators, the bill never got a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop states, companies, and individuals from interfering with doctors, nurses, and pharmacists providing reproductive health care — abortion, contraception, and IVF — that is legal in the state where it is given. It lets the Justice Department, providers, and affected people sue states to stop enforcement, bars states from using federal money to pursue such providers, requires malpractice insurers to cover them, and creates $80 million in grants for legal defense and clinic security.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients seeking abortion, contraception, or IVF care in states where that care is legal — including out-of-state patients — and the doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and clinics who serve them. Providers facing lawsuits, licensing threats, or harassment would get federal legal defense funding and security grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Reproductive care providers and their patients

how_it_helps.text: Bars any individual, entity, or state from preventing, restricting, or disadvantaging providers delivering reproductive care that is lawful in the state where it is provided, including care for patients who live elsewhere [S3].

Gives the Justice Department and private parties the power to sue states and officials to strike down violating rules, strips state sovereign immunity for such suits, and awards attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs [S3].
Prohibits states from using federal funds to pursue legal cases, disciplinary actions, or adverse licensing proceedings against providers or helpers offering lawful reproductive care [S2].
Stops medical malpractice insurers from denying coverage to, or suing, a provider solely because the provider offers lawful reproductive health care services [S2].

Creates two $40 million grant programs: one for legal defense of providers facing legal issues over abortion care, and one for clinic security including staff training, cyberattack defenses, and patient data protection [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the $80 million in grants. State governments lose the ability to use federal funds for legal cases against providers of lawful care. Malpractice insurers lose the discretion to refuse coverage based on a provider's lawful practice. Officials and private actors who enforce restrictions face lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not legalize abortion where a state has banned it — it protects only services lawful in the state where they are provided — so patients in ban states would get no new access [S3].

It overrides state authority over medical licensing and enforcement, strips state immunity from federal suit, and compels malpractice insurers to cover care they might refuse — all of which opponents view as an unacceptable federal intrusion into state regulation of medicine [S3].

It adds $80 million in new federal spending for legal defense and security grants, and protects providers from state legal action for care that is lawful locally even if many residents of that state oppose it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states where abortion and IVF remain legal, the bill offers real protection to providers whose care is under legal and physical threat, at a modest $80 million federal cost. Its biggest limitation is its scope: it cannot help patients in the states that have banned the care entirely. Its reach into state licensing and insurance regulation was certain to draw constitutional and political challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, with 27 Senate cosponsors listed at introduction [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action of any kind recorded for the bill [S5].
The bill attracted 30 cosponsors in total, 29 Democrats and 1 independent, with no Republican support [S4].
No committee action, floor vote, or companion House consideration appears in the record, and the Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials in abortion-restricting states kept their ability to pursue providers through legal and licensing actions, and malpractice insurers kept their discretion to deny coverage based on a provider's lawful practice. Patients and providers gained nothing new.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 27 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Senate cosponsors (29 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including the Judiciary Committee chairman, but the bill received no committee action.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 26, 2023, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Senate Republican minority
against.role: 49 senators, enough to block any bill through filibuster
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate majority never attempted to overcome the procedural hurdle a filibuster would have posed.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats or independents with no Republican support, and the Democratic-led committee never brought the bill to a hearing or vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Abortion and reproductive care providers (clinics, telehealth, pharmacies)
industries.note: Providers would gain federal legal protection, funded legal defense, and security grants for clinics and staff under legal or physical threat [S3]. Patients benefit because protected providers keep offering care.

The bill forbids insurers from denying professional liability coverage to, or suing, a provider solely because the provider offers lawful reproductive care, ending their ability to pressure providers that way [S2].

industries.industry: Legal services and public-interest law firms specializing in reproductive rights
industries.note: A $40 million grant program funds legal advice, representation, and compliance monitoring for providers facing legal issues over abortion care, routing work to firms with that expertise [S3].

industries.industry: Physical security and cybersecurity firms serving health facilities
industries.note: A second $40 million grant program pays for clinic security upgrades, staff training, cyberattack defenses, and patient data protection, creating demand for security vendors [S3].
